essays.title: if (document.layers): the web forks in two
essays.description: In 1997 Netscape and Microsoft each invented their own model of a web page. Everyone wrote every effect twice, and the way it ended explains a lot about how the web still works.

essays.title: Where did all the old web developers go?
essays.description: Around 2008 nobody writing JavaScript seemed to be over 40, and the industry spent a decade arguing about why. The answer was arithmetic, and the same arithmetic is running again.

essays.title: getYear() and the year 19100
essays.description: One small Date method returned 100, 2000 or 100 again for the year 2000 depending on the browser, got fixed three different ways, and is still in every browser today.

essays.title: jQuery 1.0: what $ really replaced
essays.description: jQuery 1.0 shipped in August 2006 with a dollar sign borrowed from another library, and replaced a folder of copy-pasted fixes that its own author had been winning contests with.

essays.title: View Source was the school
essays.description: For about fifteen years the web trained its own workforce through one menu item that showed how any page was made, and then the pages stopped being readable.

essays.title: Firebug: the first look inside the page
essays.description: In January 2006 one developer uploaded a few days of code as a Firefox add-on, and within a few years every browser had copied its panels, its F12 key and its console.log.
